- [fact] The bucket catalog is an in-memory cache in WiredTiger that tracks open buckets to coordinate concurrent writes. ## Structure and components

- [passage] | Field | Description | | --- | --- | | `db` | The output database name. For a [replica set](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/replication.md#std-label-replica-set) or a standalone, if the output database does not exist, `$out` also creates the database. | | `coll` | The output collection name. | | `timeseries` | A document that specifies the configuration to use when writing to a time series collection. The `timeField` is required. All other fields are optional. | | `timeField` | Required when writing to a time series collection. The name of the field which contains the date in each time series document. Documents in a time series collection must have a valid BSON date as the value for the `timeField`. | | `metaField` | Optional. The name of the field which contains metadata in each time series document. The metadata in the specified field should be data that is used to label a unique series of documents. The metadata should rarely, if ever, change The name of the specified field may not be `_id` or the same as the `timeseries.timeField`. The field can be of any data type. Although the `metaField` field is optional, using metadata can improve query optimization. For example, MongoDB automatically [creates a compound index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) on the `metaField` and `timeField` fields for new collections. If you do not provide a value for this field, the data is bucketed solely based on time. | | `granularity` | Optional. Do not use if setting `bucketRoundingSeconds` and `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`. Possible values are `seconds` (default), `minutes`, and `hours`. Set `granularity` to the value that most closely matches the time between consecutive incoming timestamps. This improves performance by optimizing how MongoDB stores data in the collection. For more information on granularity and bucket intervals, see [Set Granularity for Time Series Data.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#std-label-timeseries-granularity) | | `bucketMaxSpanSeconds` | Optional. Use with `bucketRoundingSeconds` as an alternative to `granularity`. Sets the maximum time between timestamps in the same bucket. Possible values are 1-31536000. **New in version 6.3** | | `bucketRoundingSeconds` | Optional. Use with `bucketMaxSpanSeconds` as an alternative to `granularity`. Must be equal to `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`. When a document requires a new bucket, MongoDB rounds down the document's timestamp value by this interval to set the minimum time for the bucket. **New in version 6.3** | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out.md#syntax · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, db, $out
- [passage] | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `timeseries.timeField` | string | Required. The name of the field which contains the date in each time series document. Documents in a time series collection must have a valid BSON date as the value for the `timeField`. | | `timeseries.metaField` | string | Optional. The name of the field which contains metadata in each time series document. The metadata in the specified field should be data that is used to label a unique series of documents. The metadata should rarely, if ever, change The name of the specified field may not be `_id` or the same as the `timeseries.timeField`. The field can be of any data type. Although the `metaField` field is optional, using metadata can improve query optimization. For example, MongoDB automatically [creates a compound index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) on the `metaField` and `timeField` fields for new collections. If you do not provide a value for this field, the data is bucketed solely based on time. | | `timeseries.granularity` | integer | Optional. Do not use if setting `bucketRoundingSeconds` and `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`. Possible values are `seconds` (default), `minutes`, and `hours`. Set `granularity` to the value that most closely matches the time between consecutive incoming timestamps. This improves performance by optimizing how MongoDB stores data in the collection. For more information on granularity and bucket intervals, see [Set Granularity for Time Series Data.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#std-label-timeseries-granularity) | | `timeseries.bucketMaxSpanSeconds` | integer | Optional. Use with `bucketRoundingSeconds` as an alternative to `granularity`. Sets the maximum time between timestamps in the same bucket. Possible values are 1-31536000. **New in version 6.3** | | `timeseries.bucketRoundingSeconds` | integer | Optional. Use with `bucketMaxSpanSeconds` as an alternative to `granularity`. Must be equal to `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`. When a document requires a new bucket, MongoDB rounds down the document's timestamp value by this interval to set the minimum time for the bucket. **New in version 6.3** | | `expireAfterSeconds` | integer | Optional. Enable the automatic deletion of documents in a time series collection by specifying the number of seconds after which documents expire. MongoDB deletes expired documents automatically. See [Set up Automatic Removal for Time Series Collections (TTL)](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-automatic-removal.md#std-label-manual-timeseries-automatic-removal) for more information. | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-procedures.md#time-series-field-reference · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, timeseries.timeField, timeField
- [passage] Time series documents can contain a `metaField`. MongoDB uses the `metaField` to group documents for storage optimization and query efficiency. For more information about the `metaField`, see [metaField Considerations.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#std-label-timeseries-metafield-considerations) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#metafields · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying.md

If `true` the data store is read only. Always `true` for views.; `uuid`: UUID (Universally unique identifier). Once established, the collection UUID does not change. The collection UUID remains the same across replica set members and shards in a sharded cluster. This field is only present if the collection is sharded. | | `balancingEnabledReason` | document | false, must specify [balancingConfiguration](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/listclustercatalog.md#std-label-list-cluster-catalog-balance-config) in input document | Returns information on which command has been used to toggle balancing. This document has the following fields: `enableBalancing`: `true` if [`configureCollectionBalancing`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/configurecollectionbalancing.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.configureCollectionBalancing) was used to toggle balancing; `allowMigrations`: `true` if [`setAllowMigrations`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setallowmigrations.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setAllowMigrations) was used to toggle balancing This field is only present if the collection is sharded. | | `autoMergingEnabled` | boolean | false, must specify [balancingConfiguration](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/listclustercatalog.md#std-label-list-cluster-catalog-balance-config) in input document | Specifies if the [AutoMerger](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/automerger-concept.md#std-label-automerger-concept) is enabled for the collection. - [passage] If your time series collection contains documents with `timeField` timestamps before `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` or after `2038-01-19T03:14:07.000Z`, create an index on the `timeField` to optimize queries. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#extended-date-range · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, timeField, 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z, 2038-01-19T03:14:07.000Z

- [passage] Starting in 9.0, MongoDB stores time series collections in single namespaces that contain the data compressed into organized groups, or [buckets](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#std-label-timeseries-bucketing-specifics). When you query a time series collection, MongoDB converts the data from its raw bucketed form to a logical form with one document per measurement. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#behavior · keywords: metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/
- [passage] For time series collections, the output contains `granularity`, `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`, and `bucketRoundingSeconds` parameters, if present. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#retrieve-the-current-bucketing-parameters · keywords: metaField, time series collection, granularity, bucketMaxSpanSeconds, bucketRoundingSeconds

- [passage] In this case, setting the `granularity` to `hours` groups up to a month's worth of data ingest events into a single bucket, resulting in longer traversal times and slower queries. Setting it to `seconds` leads to multiple buckets per polling interval, many of which might contain only a single document. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#set-appropriate-bucket-granularity · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, granularity, hours, seconds · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] In a regular collection, data is stored sequentially as blocks on disk, optimizing write speed. However, it requires one index for each data point, which quickly grows very large. It also requires a second index that contains the time series identifier and timestamps themselves, so that users can query for a single series. To read this data, MongoDB has to process all of the database and disk blocks that contain it, even if a block only contains a single relevant document. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#comparing-time-series-collections-to-regular-collections · keywords: index, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] If your data contains empty objects, arrays, or strings, omit the empty fields from your documents to optimize compression. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#omit-fields-containing-empty-objects-and-arrays-from-documents · keywords: metaField cardinality, working set for time series · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] If your workload has high cardinality, flattening nested objects may improve performance. For example, the following document contains the same data as the previous document but in a flattened format: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#use-standard-embedded-fields-best-practices · keywords: metaField cardinality, working set for time series · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] If the `movies` collection contains an index `{ year: 1, title: 1 }`, the following pipeline can use that index to find the first document of each group: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/group.md#optimization-to-return-the-first-or-last-document-of-each-group · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, movies, { year: 1, title: 1 }
- [passage] - Wildcard indexes are [sparse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse). They only include entries for documents that contain the indexed field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-wildcard/index-wildcard-compound.md#general-considerations-for-wildcard-indexes · keywords: index, metaField cardinality

- [passage] | `$lookup` Operation | Performance Considerations | | --- | --- | | [Equality Match with a Single Join](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/lookup.md#std-label-lookup-single-equality-example) | `$lookup` operations that perform equality matches with a single join perform better when the foreign collection contains an index on the `foreignField`.IMPORTANT: If a supporting index on the `foreignField` does not exist, a `$lookup` operation that performs an equality match with a single join likely has poor performance. | | [Uncorrelated Subqueries](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/lookup.md#std-label-lookup-uncorrelated-subquery) | `$lookup` operations that contain uncorrelated subqueries perform better when the inner pipeline can reference an index of the foreign collection.; MongoDB only needs to run the `$lookup` subquery once before caching the query because there is no relationship between the source and foreign collections. The subquery is not based on any value in the source collection. This behavior improves performance for subsequent executions of the `$lookup` operation. | | [Correlated Subqueries](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/lookup.md#std-label-lookup-concise-correlated-subquery) | `$lookup` operations that contain correlated subqueries perform better when the foreign collection contains an index on the `foreignField`.; If your pipeline passes a large number of documents to the `$lookup` query, the following strategies may improve performance:Reduce the number of documents that MongoDB passes to the `$lookup` query. For example, set a stricter filter during the `$match` stage.; Reconsider the data's schema to ensure it is optimal for the use case. | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/lookup.md#performance-considerations · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, $lookup, foreignField, $match

- [passage] | Field | Necessity | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | [field](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-field) | Required | The field to densify. The values of the specified `field` must either be all numeric values or all dates. Documents that do not contain the specified `field` continue through the pipeline unmodified. To specify a `<field>` in an embedded document or in an array, use [dot notation.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/document.md#std-label-document-dot-notation) For restrictions, see [`field` Restrictions.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-field-restrictions) | | [partitionByFields](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-partition-by-fields) | Optional | The set of fields to act as the compound key to group the documents. In the [`$densify`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-densify) stage, each group of documents is known as a *partition*. If you omit this field, [`$densify`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-densify) uses one partition for the entire collection. For an example, see [Densification with Partitions.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-examples-partitions) For restrictions, see [`partitionByFields` Restrictions.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-partition-by-fields-restrictions) | | [range](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-range) | Required | An object that specifies how the data is densified. | | [range.bounds](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-bounds) | Required | You can specify `range.bounds` as either: An array: `[ < lower bound >, < upper bound > ]`,; A string: either `"full"` or `"partition"`. If `bounds` is an array: [`$densify`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-densify) adds documents spanning the range of values within the specified bounds.; The data type for the bounds must correspond to the data type in the [field](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-field) being densified.; For behavior details, see [`range.bounds` Behavior.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-bounds-behavior) If `bounds` is `"full"`: [`$densify`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-densify) adds documents spanning the full range of values of the `field` being densified. If `bounds` is `"partition"`: [`$densify`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-densify) adds documents to each partition, similar to if you had run a `full` range densification on each partition individually. | | [range.step](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-step) | Required | The amount to increment the [field](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-field) value in each document. [`$densify`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-densify) creates a new document for each `step` between the existing documents. If [range.unit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-unit) is specified, `step` must be an integer. Otherwise, `step` can be any numeric value. | | [range.unit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-unit) | Required if [field](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-field) is a date. | The unit to apply to the [step](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-step) field when incrementing date values in [field.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-field) You can specify one of the following values for `unit` as a string: `millisecond`; `second`; `minute`; `hour`; `day`; `week`; `month`; `quarter`; `year` For an example, see [Densify Time Series Data.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#std-label-densify-examples-time-series) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/densify.md#syntax · keywords: time series collection, field, <field>, $densify, partitionByFields, range.bounds

- [passage] | Aspect | Atlas Core | Atlas Infinite | | --- | --- | --- | | Architecture | Compute and storage run on the same node. Each data-bearing node runs on a virtual machine with attached storage. | Compute and storage run as independent layers. MongoDB manages the storage layer separately from the compute nodes. | | Compute scaling | You change compute capacity by selecting a different cluster tier. Atlas restarts the cluster's nodes when you change the tier, with no downtime on dedicated clusters. | You scale the cluster tier independently of storage. Scaling doesn't move your data, so it is fast. | | Storage scaling | You scale storage capacity and IOPS independently of compute on dedicated clusters, up to the maximum for the cluster tier. To add capacity beyond that maximum, you scale to a higher tier. | Storage capacity increases automatically based on usage, independently of the cluster tier, without downtime. | | Horizontal scaling | You shard a cluster when its data approaches the storage capacity, and add workload-specific nodes, like read-only or analytics nodes, as needed. | Higher storage capacity means you can store up to 128TB on a single shard without sharding. Adding workload-specific nodes is much faster. | | Recovery | Atlas monitors your database regularly, and performs auto-healing if it discovers an issue. If it replaces a node, the new node performs an initial sync before it serves queries. | Atlas monitors your database regularly, and performs auto-healing if it discovers an issue. If it replaces a node, the new node immediately connects to the storage layer, with no need for an initial sync. | | Cloud provider and tier availability | Free clusters, Flex clusters, and dedicated cluster tiers, on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. | Public preview: `M10` through `M60` replica sets in supported AWS regions, with storage capacity up to 128 TB per replica set. | | Feature coverage | Supports the full Atlas feature set. | Some Atlas features aren't [supported during public preview.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/infinite/atlas-infinite-landing.md#std-label-atlas-infinite-availability) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/index.md#compare-editions · keywords: working set for time series, M10, M60
- [passage] Messages related to compaction operations performed by the [WiredTiger](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger.md#std-label-storage-wiredtiger) storage engine. To specify the log level for [`WTCMPCT`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#mongodb-data-WTCMPCT) components, use the [`systemLog.component.storage.wt.wtCompact.verbosity`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-systemLog.component.storage.wt.wtCompact.verbosity) setting. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#components · keywords: working set for time series, WTCMPCT, systemLog.component.storage.wt.wtCompact.verbosity
- [passage] Sharding distributes data across the shards in the cluster, allowing each shard to contain a subset of the total cluster data. As the data set grows, additional shards increase the storage capacity of the cluster. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sharding/ · keywords: working set for time series

## How it works

- [passage] Last point queries are most performant when they use the [DISTINCT\_SCAN optimization](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-results). This optimization is only available when an index on `timeField` is descending. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, timeField
- [statement] Last-point queries (latest measurement per metaField value) use $sort { meta: 1, time: -1 } then $group with $first. They are fastest with DISTINCT_SCAN, which the docs say is available only when the index on timeField is descending; confirm via explain('executionStats') showing DISTINCT_SCAN. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns
- [statement] Because buckets group by exact metaField value, many unique metaField values produce many sparse buckets, which lowers query efficiency; pushdown then prunes fewer useful buckets. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [fact] Sort on {timeField: ±1} uses a secondary index on the timeField. Sort on {metaField: ±1, timeField: ±1} uses the default compound index. A sort on the timeField uses a {metaField, timeField} index when the query has a point predicate on the metaField. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [statement] Explain output for a time series query shows a $_internalUnpackBucket stage and, even when the predicate was pushed down, a separate $match stage still appears afterward to re-check unpacked documents. Do not read the residual $match as proof that pushdown failed. — https://levelup.gitconnected.com/how-mongodb-time-series-collection-works-under-the-hood-2348f3a2318e · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [fact] Per MongoDB docs, a sort on { timeField: ±1 } uses a secondary index on timeField; a sort on { metaField: ±1, timeField: ±1 } uses the default compound index; a sort on { timeField: ±1 } uses a { metaField, timeField } compound index only when the query has a point predicate on metaField. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns
- [passage] - If there are secondary indexes for the clustered collection, the collection has a larger storage size. This is because secondary indexes on a clustered collection with large clustered index keys may have a larger storage size than secondary indexes on a non-clustered collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#limitations · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, secondary index on time series, working set for time series
- [passage] MongoDB uses the `metaField` to partition data for efficient organization and retrieval. When you create a time series collection, MongoDB groups documents into buckets. Documents within a bucket share an identical `metaField` value and have `timeField` values that are close together. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#metafield-considerations · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, timeField
- [passage] When you insert data into a time series collection, the internal collection automatically organizes the data into an optimized storage format using [buckets](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#std-label-timeseries-bucketing-specifics). If a suitable bucket exists, MongoDB inserts new data into that bucket. If a suitable bucket does not exist, MongoDB creates a new bucket. To optimize storage, choose a `metaField` that rarely changes to create time series collections with fewer, more densely packed buckets. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#storage-and-cardinality · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection
- [passage] When you create a time series collection, MongoDB groups incoming time series data into buckets. By accurately setting granularity, you control how frequently data is bucketed based on the ingestion rate of your data. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#set-appropriate-bucket-granularity · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md
- [passage] All time series collection use a compressed bucket format when you append data into opened or reopened buckets. Compressing time series data in the cache supports high [cardinality](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-cardinality) workloads while preserving efficient query performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#compression-and-hardware · keywords: metaField cardinality, time series collection, working set for time series
- [passage] Index hints cause MongoDB to use a specific index for a query. Some operations on time series collections can only take advantage of an index if that index is specified in a hint. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#specify-index-hints-for-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [passage] For example, the following query causes MongoDB to use the `timestamp_1_metadata.sensorId_1` index: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#specify-index-hints-for-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, timestamp_1_metadata.sensorId_1
- [passage] The Query Profiler samples operations by using a bucketing algorithm that adjusts the sample size based on the width of the selected time range. Because of differences in bucket size, a wider time range might display fewer sampled operations than a narrower time range. For exact, unsampled operation counts, download your `mongod` logs. To learn more, see [View and Download MongoDB Logs.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/mongodb-logs.md#std-label-mongodb-logs) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/query-profiler.md#data-display-limitations · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, working set for time series, mongod · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/query-profiler/
- [fact] Bucket count depends on the number of unique metaField values, because documents share a bucket only if their metaField values match exactly (for object/array metaFields, all fields/elements must match). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, working set for time series, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [fact] Some operations on a time series collection only use an index when it is passed as a hint. A hint can be an index name or a key pattern. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] Working set is the subset of data and indexes touched in a typical window, rarely the whole database. Practitioner guidance is to size the cache to working set plus write headroom, and to use a sustained post-warmup page-fault rate as a proxy when the size is unknown. — https://www.netdata.cloud/guides/mongodb/mongodb-cache-undersized-working-set/ · keywords: index, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series
- [passage] `{ metaField: ±1, timeField: ±1 }` when there is a point predicate on `<metaField>` — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#use-secondary-indexes-to-improve-sort-performance · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, { metaField: ±1, timeField: ±1 }, <metaField>
- [passage] MongoDB begins removing expired documents or time series buckets as soon as the index finishes building on the [primary](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-primary). For more information on the index build process, see [Index Builds on Populated Collections.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-creation.md#std-label-index-operations) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl.md#timing-of-the-delete-operation · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/
- [passage] You can specify a `partialFilterExpression` option for all MongoDB [index types](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types.md#std-label-index-types). When specifying a `partialFilterExpression` for a TTL index on a time series collection, you can only filter on the collection `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#create-a-partial-index · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, partialFilterExpression
- [passage] 3. Optionally, set `ExpireAfter` to expire documents when the value of the `timeField` reaches the specified interval. Expired documents are automatically deleted: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-procedures.md#configure-a-time-series-collection · keywords: metaField, time series collection, ExpireAfter, timeField
- [passage] Optionally, set `expireAfter` to expire documents when the value of the `timeField` reaches the specified interval. Expired documents are automatically deleted. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-procedures.md#configure-a-time-series-collection · keywords: metaField, time series collection, expireAfter, timeField

- [statement] During 8.0 development, Jira SERVER-88316 (fixed in 8.0.0-rc0) showed the server using block processing for a GroupByNull test case with only featureFlagSbeFull set, when the test expected none. This shows the block-processing decision depended on several feature flags. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-88316 · keywords: block processing, time series collection, MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing (time series)

- [passage] `coordinates` fields with populated values and `coordinates` fields with an empty array result in a schema change for the compressor. The schema change causes the second and third documents in the sequence to remain uncompressed. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#omit-fields-containing-empty-objects-and-arrays-from-documents · keywords: metaField cardinality, working set for time series, coordinates
- [passage] In some instances, such as when running in a container that is configured to use less RAM than the amount of memory provisioned for the host, you must account for the limits. You may need to configure the WiredTiger cache to an appropriate value, as WiredTiger may not account for the memory limits of the specific container in certain cases. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#wiredtiger-options · keywords: working set for time series, metaField cardinality · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md
- [passage] When using encryption, CPUs equipped with AES-NI instruction-set extensions show significant performance advantages. If you are using MongoDB Enterprise with the [Encrypted Storage Engine](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/security-encryption-at-rest.md#std-label-encrypted-storage-engine), choose a CPU that supports AES-NI for better performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#compression-and-encryption · keywords: metaField cardinality, working set for time series
- [passage] Collections with fine-grained or changing `metaField` values generate many sparsely packed, short-lived buckets, increasing the cardinality of your collection. Increasing cardinality leads to decreased storage and query efficiency. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#storage-and-cardinality · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality
- [fact] Granularity must match per-source ingest interval: 'seconds' (1h bucket span) with sparse data leads to buckets with a single document; 'hours' (30-day span) leads to longer traversal. Custom bucketMaxSpanSeconds/bucketRoundingSeconds exist since 6.3. Granularity mismatch compounds metaField cardinality fragmentation. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [passage] - In [time series collections](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#std-label-manual-timeseries-collection), documents do not require a unique [\_id](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-_id) field because MongoDB does not create an index on the `_id` field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#properties-of-time-series-data · keywords: index, time series collection, _id
- [passage] In time series collections, documents do not require a unique _id field because MongoDB does not create an index on the _id field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/ · keywords: index, time series collection
- [passage] For every encrypted collection, MongoDB creates [two metadata collections](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#std-label-qe-metadata-collections), increasing storage space. MongoDB creates an index for each encrypted field, which increases the duration of write operations on that field. When a write operation updates an indexed field, MongoDB updates the related index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/encrypt-and-query.md#considerations-when-enabling-querying · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] - Create the indexes that the Performance Advisor suggests when they align with your [Indexing Strategies.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/applications/indexes/) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/analyze-slow-queries.md#best-practices-for-query-performance · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] The [`sh.shardCollection()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/sh.shardcollection.md#mongodb-method-sh.shardCollection) method can also create a unique index on the shard key when passed the `{ unique: true }` option if: the shard key is [range-based](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/ranged-sharding.md), the collection is empty, and a unique index on the shard key doesn't already exist. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#output-to-a-sharded-collection · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, sh.shardCollection(), { unique: true }

- [passage] `notablescan` does not allow unbounded queries that use a clustered index because the queries require a full collection scan. - [passage] You can only have one clustered index in a collection because the documents can be stored in only one order. - [passage] - A clustered index can only be created when you create the collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#behavior · keywords: index, secondary index on time series
- [passage] Starting in MongoDB 6.0.7, if a usable clustered index exists, the MongoDB query planner evaluates the clustered index against secondary indexes in the query planning process. - [passage] | Counter | Description | | --- | --- | | `collscan``clusteredCollscan` | Collection scans, counted separately based on whether the scan uses the [clustered index.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#std-label-clustered-collections) | | `coveredIxscan` | Index scans that don't fetch documents. | | `ixscanFetch` | Index scans that fetch documents. | | `countScan` | Scans that count index keys without returning documents. | | `distinctScan``distinctScanFetch` | Scans that skip duplicate index keys, counted separately based on whether the scan fetches documents. | | `geoNear2d``geoNear2dSphere` | Geospatial proximity searches, counted separately based on whether the query uses a [2d](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d.md#std-label-2d-index) or [2dsphere](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2dsphere.md#std-label-2dsphere-index) index. | | `textMatch` | Text searches that use a [text index.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-text.md#std-label-index-type-text) | | `otherAccessPath` | Winning plans that don't use a collection scan, an index scan, a count scan, a distinct scan, or a geospatial access path. A plan that only performs a text search increments both `textMatch` and `otherAccessPath`. | | `btreeIxscan``wildcardIxscan``sparseIxscan``uniqueIxscan``hashedIxscan``multikeyIxscan` | Index scans, counted separately by index property. A single index scan can increment multiple of these counters. | | `boundsFullScan``boundsPoint``boundsBoundedRange``boundsMinKeyToValue``boundsValueToMaxKey``boundsMixture` | Index scans, counted separately by the index bounds that the scan uses. MongoDB increments `boundsMixture` when the scan uses more than one type of bound. | | `boundsUnionedSmall``boundsUnionedLarge` | Index scans where a field has multiple bounds, counted separately by the number of bounds. `boundsUnionedSmall` counts fields with 2 to 50 bounds, and `boundsUnionedLarge` counts fields with 51 or more bounds. | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/queryStats.md#access-path-counters · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, collscan, clusteredCollscan, coveredIxscan, ixscanFetch

- [passage] Enabling Queryable Encryption on a collection redacts fields from some diagnostic commands and omits some operations from the query log. This limits the data available to MongoDB support engineers, especially when analyzing query performance. To measure the impact of operations against encrypted collections, use a third party application performance monitoring tool to collect metrics. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/reference/compatibility.md#mongodb-support-limitations · keywords: metaField cardinality · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/reference/limitations.md
- [passage] `$group` is a blocking stage, which causes the pipeline to wait for all input data to be retrieved for the blocking stage before processing the data. A blocking stage may reduce performance because it reduces parallel processing for a pipeline with multiple stages. A blocking stage may also use substantial amounts of memory for large data sets. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/group.md#performance · keywords: metaField cardinality, $group

- [passage] - Only one array field should appear in the [query document](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/query-documents.md#std-label-read-operations-query-argument). Additional array fields in the query document may lead to undefined behavior. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/positional.md#array-field-limitations · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] When used as an accumulator, `$median` always uses an approximation algorithm. As a result, the computed percentiles `$median` returns on the same data set might differ on each run, due to pseudorandomness in the t-digest approximation algorithm. Additionally, `$median` may return a value that differs slightly from the true statistical median. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/median.md#calculation-considerations · keywords: metaField cardinality, $median
- [passage] Because CSFLE and Queryable Encryption do not provide a mechanism to verify the integrity of a schema, relying on a server-side schema means trusting that the server's schema has not been tampered with. If an adversary compromises the server, they can modify the schema so that a previously encrypted field is no longer labeled for encryption. This causes the client to send plaintext values for that field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/about-qe-csfle.md#security-considerations · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] - When a whole array is sorted, the sort is lexicographic. See [`$sort`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sort.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-sort) for more details. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sortArray.md#considerations · keywords: metaField cardinality, $sort

- [passage] If you're connecting to a multi-cloud MongoDB Atlas deployment through a [private connection](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/faq/connection-changes.md#std-label-conn-string-options), you can access only the nodes in the same cloud provider that you're connecting from. - [passage] When inserting documents with monotonically increasing shard keys, all inserts belong to the same [chunk](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-chunk) on a single [shard](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-shard). The system eventually divides the chunk range that receives all write operations and migrates its contents to distribute data more evenly. However, at any moment the cluster directs insert operations only to a single shard, which creates an insert throughput bottleneck. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/limits.md#shard-key-limitations · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] - [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod) includes a [Full Time Diagnostic Data Capture](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/full-time-diagnostic-data-capture.md#std-label-ftdc-stub) mechanism to assist MongoDB engineers with troubleshooting deployments. If this thread fails, it terminates the originating process. To avoid the most common failures, confirm that the user running the process has permissions to create the FTDC `diagnostic.data` directory. For `mongod` the directory is within [`storage.dbPath`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-storage.dbPath). For `mongos` it is parallel to [`systemLog.path`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-systemLog.path) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#considerations · keywords: metaField cardinality, mongod, diagnostic.data, storage.dbPath, mongos, systemLog.path

- [passage] For example, in the following aggregation pipeline, [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) excludes the `_id` field from the documents passed into `$merge`. When `$merge` writes these documents to the `"newCollection"`, `$merge` generates a new `_id` field and value. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#id-field-generation · keywords: metaField cardinality, $project, _id, $merge, "newCollection"
- [passage] The `$merge` stage can output to a sharded collection. When the output collection is sharded, `$merge` uses the `_id` field and all the [shard key](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-shard-key.md#std-label-sharding-shard-key-creation) fields as the default [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) identifier. If you override the default, the [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) identifier must include all the [shard key](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-shard-key.md#std-label-sharding-shard-key-creation) fields: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#output-to-a-sharded-collection · keywords: metaField cardinality, $merge, _id
- [passage] When [`$merge`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-merge) outputs to the same collection that is being aggregated, documents may get updated multiple times or the operation may result in an infinite loop. This behavior occurs when the update performed by [`$merge`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-merge) changes the physical location of documents stored on disk. When the physical location of a document changes, [`$merge`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-merge) may view it as an entirely new document, resulting in additional updates. For more information on this behavior, see [Halloween Problem.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween_Problem) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#output-to-the-same-collection-that-is-being-aggregated · keywords: metaField cardinality, $merge
- [passage] When used as an accumulator, `$percentile` always uses an approximation algorithm. Additionally, `$percentile` may return values that differ slightly from the true statistical percentiles. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/percentile.md#calculation-considerations · keywords: metaField cardinality, $percentile
- [passage] - Atlas displays top namespaces by default. Depending on the time range, a namespace might fall in and out of the monitored list. - [passage] The `numad` daemon process can also reduce [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod) performance. - [passage] MongoDB performs best where swapping can be avoided or kept to a minimum, as retrieving data from swap will always be slower than accessing data in RAM. However, if the system hosting MongoDB runs out of RAM, swapping can prevent the Linux OOM Killer from terminating the [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod) process. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#swap · keywords: metaField cardinality, mongod
- [passage] With the WiredTiger storage engine, WiredTiger objects may be stored on remote file systems if the remote file system conforms to ISO/IEC 9945-1:1996 (POSIX.1). Because remote file systems are often slower than local file systems, using a remote file system for storage may degrade performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#remote-filesystems-nfs · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] When running MongoDB in production on Linux, you should use Linux kernel version 2.6.36 or later, with either the XFS or EXT4 filesystem. If possible, use XFS as it generally performs better with MongoDB. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#kernel-and-file-systems · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] With the [WiredTiger storage engine](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger.md#std-label-storage-wiredtiger), using XFS is **strongly recommended** for data bearing nodes to avoid performance issues that may occur when using EXT4 with WiredTiger. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#kernel-and-file-systems · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] - Adjust the `ulimit` settings for your platform according to the recommendations in the [ulimit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/ulimit.md#std-label-ulimit) reference. Low `ulimit` values will negatively affect MongoDB when under heavy use and can lead to failed connections to MongoDB processes and loss of service. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#recommended-configuration · keywords: metaField cardinality, ulimit
- [passage] Higher readahead commonly benefits sequential I/O operations. Because MongoDB disk access patterns are generally random, if you use higher readahead settings you get limited benefit and it can degrade performance. For optimal MongoDB performance, set readahead between 8 and 32, unless testing shows a measurable, repeatable, and reliable benefit from a higher value. [MongoDB commercial support](https://support.mongodb.com/welcome) can advise on alternate readahead configurations. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#recommended-configuration · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] VMware supports *memory overcommitment*, where you can assign more memory to your virtual machines than the physical machine has available. When memory is overcommitted, the hypervisor reallocates memory between the virtual machines. VMware's balloon driver (`vmmemctl`) reclaims the pages that are considered least valuable. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#vmware · keywords: metaField cardinality, vmmemctl
- [passage] The balloon driver resides inside the guest operating system. Under certain configurations, when the balloon driver expands, it can interfere with MongoDB's memory management and affect MongoDB's performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#vmware · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] You should also consider typical queries when choosing the `granularity` value. For example, if you expect your queries to fetch 1 day of data at a time, use "minutes". A finer granularity, like "seconds", creates buckets that cover one hour. This requires more buckets to represent the same data, which negatively affects storage and query performance. A coarser granularity, like "hours" (which has a 30-day bucket span), requires queries to fetch 30 days of data at a time and then filter out most of it. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#granularity · keywords: metaField, granularity
- [passage] For each open bucket, the catalog maintains information such as the `metaField`, active writers, covered time span, number of documents, size, and recent operations. Because MongoDB creates separate buckets for documents with a different `metaField`, multiple buckets are typically open at the same time. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#the-bucket-catalog · keywords: metaField · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/

- [passage] - Use an odd number of voting members to ensure that elections proceed successfully. You can have up to 7 voting members. If you have an *even* number of voting members, and constraints, such as cost, prohibit adding another secondary to be a voting member, you can add an [arbiter](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-arbiter) to ensure an odd number of votes. For additional considerations when using an arbiter for a 3-member replica set (P-S-A), see [Replica Set Arbiter.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-arbiter.md) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-checklist-development.md#replication · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] When using [Queryable Encryption](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption.md#std-label-qe-manual-feature-qe), CRUD operations against encrypted collections are omitted from the [`system.profile`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/system-collections.md#mongodb-data--database-.system.profile) collection. For details, see [Redaction.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/reference/limitations.md#std-label-qe-redaction) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md · keywords: metaField cardinality, system.profile · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md
- [passage] Free clusters and Flex clusters only trigger alerts related to the metrics supported by those clusters. For complete documentation on Free clusters and Flex clusters alert and metric limitations, see [Atlas Free Cluster Limits](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations.md#std-label-atlas-free-tier), and [Atlas Flex Limitations.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/flex-limitations.md#std-label-flex-cluster-limitations) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/configure-alerts.md · keywords: metaField cardinality · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/alerts.md
- [passage] These enhancements further reduce size of data on disk when compressed with `zstd`, and also significantly reduce space used in the WiredTiger cache. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-compression.md#column-compression · keywords: working set for time series, zstd
- [passage] This section describes considerations when running MongoDB in some of the more common virtual environments. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#mongodb-on-virtual-environments · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] Specify the `encryptedFieldsObject` when you create the collection, and also when you create a client to access the collection. For more information about the security considerations of not defining the `encryptedFieldsObject`, see [Security Considerations.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/about-qe-csfle.md#std-label-qe-csfle-security-considerations) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/enable-qe.md#enable-queryable-encryption-on-a-collection · keywords: metaField cardinality, encryptedFieldsObject

## How-to and procedures

- [passage] To improve query performance, [create one or more secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) on your `timeField` and `metaField` to support common query patterns. In versions 6.3 and higher, MongoDB creates a secondary index on the `timeField` and `metaField` automatically. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#create-secondary-indexes · keywords: index, metaField, metaField cardinality, secondary index on time series, time series collection, timeField · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] To improve query performance for [time series collections](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-time-series-collection), add one or more [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index) to support common time series query patterns. Starting in MongoDB 6.3, MongoDB automatically creates a [compound index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#std-label-index-type-compound) on the `metaField` and `timeField` fields for new collections. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, timeField · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md
- [passage] To confirm that the last point query used the secondary index, run the operation again using `explain`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, explain
- [passage] To confirm that the last point query used the secondary index, run the operation again using `.explain( "executionStats" )`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, .explain( "executionStats" )
- [passage] To learn how to optimize compression, see [Compression Best Practices.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#std-label-tsc-best-practice-optimize-compression) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-compression.md#learn-more · keywords: metaField cardinality, time series collection, working set for time series
- [passage] To improve query performance, you can manually [add secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) to any field in your time series collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [passage] To convert a collection from custom bucketing to a `granularity`, value, both `bucketMaxSpanSeconds` and `bucketRoundingSeconds` must be less than or equal to the `granularity` equivalent: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collMod.md#modify-time-series-collections · keywords: metaField, time series collection, granularity, bucketMaxSpanSeconds, bucketRoundingSeconds
- [passage] To learn how to optimize inserts for large operations, see [Inserts Best Practices.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#std-label-tsc-best-practice-optimize-inserts) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-procedures.md#insert-measurements-into-a-time-series-collection · keywords: metaField cardinality, time series collection
- [passage] To query the `metaField` for a single time series: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-quick-start.md · keywords: metaField, time series collection

- [passage] To modify the granularity of a **sharded** time series collection, you must be running MongoDB 6.0 or later. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#change-time-series-granularity · keywords: metaField, time series collection
- [passage] Use the [`shardCollection()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/sh.shardcollection.md#mongodb-method-sh.shardCollection) method with the [timeseries](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/sh.shardcollection.md#std-label-method-sharded-time-series-collection-options) option. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-shard-collection.md#create-a-sharded-time-series-collection · keywords: time series collection, time series sharding, shardCollection()

- [passage] Ensure that your [oplog](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-oplog) is large enough to permit the indexing or re-indexing operation to complete without falling too far behind to catch up. - [passage] To use custom bucketing parameters, set both parameters to the same value, and do not set `granularity`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#using-custom-bucketing-parameters · keywords: metaField, granularity
- [passage] Set `granularity` to `R5`, `R10`, `R20`, `R40`, or `R80` to restrict bucket boundaries to values in the series. The values of the series are multiplied by a power of 10 when the `groupBy` values are outside of the 1.0 to 10.0 (10.3 for `R80`) range. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/bucketAuto.md#renard-series · keywords: metaField, granularity, R5, R10, R20, R40
- [passage] Set `granularity` to `E6`, `E12`, `E24`, `E48`, `E96`, or `E192` to restrict bucket boundaries to values in the series. The values of the series are multiplied by a power of 10 when the `groupBy` values are outside of the 1.0 to 10.0 range. To learn more about the E-series and their respective relative errors, see [preferred number series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preferred_number). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/bucketAuto.md#e-series · keywords: metaField, granularity, E6, E12, E24, E48
- [passage] Set `granularity` to `1-2-5` to restrict bucket boundaries to various powers of the third root of 10, rounded to one significant digit. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/bucketAuto.md#1-2-5-series · keywords: metaField, granularity, 1-2-5
- [passage] Set `granularity` to `POWERSOF2` to restrict bucket boundaries to numbers that are a power of two. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/bucketAuto.md#powers-of-two-series · keywords: metaField, granularity, POWERSOF2
- [passage] To view the `scoreDetails` metadata field, you must either: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/score.md#scoredetails · keywords: metaField, scoreDetails · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/rankFusion.md
- [passage] Avoid specifying **only** the `timeField` as the shard key. Since the `timeField` [increases monotonically](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key.md#std-label-shard-key-monotonic), it may result in all writes appearing on a single chunk within the cluster. Ideally, data is evenly distributed across chunks. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#shard-key-fields · keywords: metaField, timeField
- [passage] Set a Strategic metaField When Creating the Collection — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/ · keywords: metaField
- [passage] To reduce the size of the `ESC` metadata collection by at least `t` documents, run metadata compaction when the following formula is satisfied: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#scheduling-metadata-compaction · keywords: working set for time series, ESC
- [passage] Use [`mongostat`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/database-tools/mongostat.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongostat) to understand the distribution of operation types and to inform capacity planning. See the [`mongostat`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/database-tools/mongostat.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongostat) reference page for details. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/monitoring.md#mongostat · keywords: working set for time series, mongostat
- [passage] Use this data to monitor the state and storage capacity of a specific database. This output also allows you to compare use between databases and to determine the average [document](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-document) size in a database. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/monitoring.md#dbstats · keywords: working set for time series
- [passage] Use Standard Embedded Fields Best Practices — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/ · keywords: metaField cardinality

## Measurements and reference values

- [fact] The official docs make no numeric performance claim. They say only that the gain varies with workload and instance configuration. The vendor blog's 10-100x figures are therefore workload-specific best cases and should not be assumed for other pipelines. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.2/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying/ · keywords: block processing, metaField cardinality, time series collection, MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing (time series)
- [fact] A bucket closes when the set of active buckets does not fit within the allowed storage engine cache size, or when the bucket catalog exceeds its memory allocation (default 2.5% of system memory). The docs point to collStats for reviewing this. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/ · keywords: metaField, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series
- [passage] For any configuration of granularity parameters, the maximum size of a bucket is 1000 measurements or 125KB of data, whichever is lower. MongoDB may also enforce a lower maximum size for high cardinality data with many unique values, so that the working set of buckets fits within the [WiredTiger cache.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger.md#std-label-storage-wiredtiger) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#bucket-size · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, working set for time series
- [statement] A MongoDB staff forum answer (March 2022) gave an informal rule of thumb of RAM at 15-20% of total data size, covering indexes, working set, queries and OS. It is not an official time-series formula and cites MongoDB 4.0 docs. — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/working-set-should-be-sized-to-fit-into-ram-or-wiredtiger-internal-cache/140684 · keywords: index, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series
- [fact] A new bucket is created when the metaField matches no active bucket, the timestamp is outside all active buckets' ranges, or the doc exceeds remaining size/count limits. Buckets close at 1000 docs by default, 125KiB size cap, when the active bucket set exceeds storage-engine cache, or when the bucket catalog exceeds its memory allocation (default 2.5% of system memory). High cardinality means many open buckets and so earlier closures. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [statement] Community report: on 6.0.5 with metaField=userid, granularity=hours, ~40B events/3TB, reads and writes degraded after ~3 weeks; one user had 3,120 buckets for 20,539 docs, dropping to 370 after read/delete/re-insert, giving >10x faster queries. A second user reported ~10s for a project/group over ~6M records. No MongoDB staff answer or confirmed fix in the thread. — https://mongodb.com/community/forums/t/mongodb-v6-0-time-series-slowness-issue/283439 · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [passage] For example, on a system with a total of 4GB of RAM the WiredTiger cache uses 1.5GB of RAM (`0.5 * (4GB - 1GB) = 1.5 GB`). When providing a specific cache size ensure the RAM does not exceed the bounds of 0.256GB to 10000GB. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#cache-configuration-settings · keywords: metaField cardinality, working set for time series, 0.5 * (4GB - 1GB) = 1.5 GB
- [statement] A forum report with indexes on t/c in both directions shows a range filter { c: x, t: { $lte: ... } } with sort { t: -1 } spending IXSCAN ~4s but FETCH ~2-5 minutes, while a similar $gte ascending query took ~1s; no answer was given, version unstated. — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/filter-on-time-series-with-lte-on-timestamp-and-reverse-index-is-too-slow/296074 · keywords: index, time series collection, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns
- [passage] - A clustered index supports keys up to 8 MB in size, but a much smaller clustered index key is best. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#set-your-own-clustered-index-key-values · keywords: index, secondary index on time series
- [passage] The maximum size for documents within a time series collection is 4 MB. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#document-size · keywords: time series collection
- [passage] Commodity (SATA) spinning drives are often a good option, as the random I/O performance increase with more expensive spinning drives is not that dramatic (only on the order of 2x). Using SSDs or increasing RAM may be more effective in increasing I/O throughput. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#use-solid-state-disks-ssds · keywords: metaField cardinality
- [passage] - The bucket catalog exceeds its allowed total memory allocation (by default, 2.5% of available system memory) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#closure · keywords: metaField · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] - If your WiredTiger cache fill ratio regularly exceeds 90% — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/build-indexes-on-replica-sets.md#about-this-task · keywords: working set for time series
- [passage] Manually run [metadata collection compaction](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#std-label-qe-metadata-compaction) when your metadata collections exceed 1 GB. Compaction decreases the size of the metadata collections associated with encrypted fields, and improves performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/reference/limitations.md#manual-metadata-collection-compaction · keywords: working set for time series

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [fact] Since MongoDB 6.3 the server automatically creates a compound index on the metaField and timeField for new time series collections. No index exists on _id; a hint on _id fails unless the user creates that index, and in 8.3 an index or hint named "_id_" returns an error. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] Partial indexes work on time series collections. Since 6.0 they accept $or, $in and $geoWithin, but cannot be created on the metaField and timeField. Since 7.0 a TTL index with a partialFilterExpression that depends only on the metaField is allowed. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] distinct() cannot be efficiently indexed on time series collections; use $match on a metaField prefix with $group over a compound metaField index instead. For high-cardinality workloads, flattening nested measurement objects may help, but docs recommend it only if nesting causes significant performance issues. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: index, metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [fact] On MongoDB 5.0.3, sorting a 10M-document time series collection by timestamp with no index failed with 'Sort exceeded memory limit of 104857600 bytes, but did not opt in to external sorting'; the author had to add an index to sort by time. — https://blog.allegro.tech/2021/12/performance-evaluation-of-timeseries.html · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns
- [passage] If your time series collection includes `timeField` values before `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` or after `2038-01-19T03:14:07.000Z`, MongoDB logs a warning and disables some query optimizations that make use of the [internal clustered index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#std-label-manual-timeseries-internal-index). To regain query performance and resolve the log warning, [create a secondary index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) on the `timeField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-migrate-with-aggregation.md#next-steps · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, timeField, 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-migrate-with-tools.md
- [passage] MongoDB automatically enables block processing for eligible time series queries. You cannot manually specify whether a query uses block processing. - [passage] A `metaField` should rarely change and can be any data type. A `metaField` can be an object and can contain subfields. Once you define a field as the `metaField`, you can change the value of the `metaField` but you cannot redefine the `metaField` as another field. For example, if you create time series documents with the `metaField` defined as field `A`, you cannot later convert a field `B` to be the `metaField`. However, if the value of `A` is an object, you can add new subfields to `A`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#metafield-considerations · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, , you cannot later convert a field ,  to be the , . - [passage] | Metric | Description | | --- | --- | | `numBuckets` | The total number of tracked buckets. Expected to be equal to the sum of `numOpenBuckets` and `numArchivedBuckets`. | | `numOpenBuckets` | The number of tracked buckets with a full representation stored in-cache, ready to receive new documents. | | `numIdleBuckets` | The number of buckets that are open and currently without an uncommitted document insertion pending. buckets. | | `numBucketsClosedDueToCount` | The number of buckets closed due to reaching their document count limit. | | `numBucketsClosedDueToSchemaChange` | The number of buckets closed because the schema of an incoming document was incompatible with that of the documents in the open bucket. | | `numBucketsClosedDueToSize` | The number of buckets closed because an incoming document would make that `metaField` value. | | `numBucketsReopened` | The number of buckets re-opened because a document arrived that didn't match any open buckets, but did match an existing non-full bucket. | | `numBucketsKeptOpenDueToLargeMeasurements` | The number of buckets that would have been closed due size, but were kept open due to not containing a minimum number of documents required to achieve reasonable compression. | | `numBucketsClosedDueToCachePressure` | The number of buckets closed because their size exceeds the bucket catalog's dynamic [bucket size
