This limit is distinct from the maximum bucket size limit. | | `numBucketsFrozen` | The number of frozen buckets. Buckets are frozen if attempting to compress the bucket would corrupt its contents. | | `numCompressedBucketsConvertedToUnsorted` | The number of compressed buckets that contain documents not sorted by their respective `timeField` values. | | `numBucketsFetched` | The number of archived buckets fetched to check if they were suitable for re-opening. | | `numBucketsQueried` | The total number of buckets queried to see if they could hold an incoming document. | | `numBucketFetchesFailed` | The number of archived buckets fetched that were not suitable for re-opening. | | `numBucketQueriesFailed` | The number of queries for a suitable open bucket that failed due to lack of candidate availability. | | `numBucketReopeningsFailed` | The number of attempted bucket reopenings that failed due to reasons including conflicts with concurrent operations, malformed buckets, and more. | | `numDuplicateBucketsReopened` | The number of re-opened buckets that are duplicates of currently open buckets. | | `stateManagement` | A document that tracks bucket catalog state information. | | `stateManagement.bucketsManaged` | The total number of buckets that are being tracked for conflict management. This includes open buckets in the bucket catalog and any buckets that are being directly written to, including by update and delete commands. | | `stateManagement.currentEra` | The current era of the bucket catalog. The bucket catalog starts at era 0 and increments when a bucket is cleared. Attempting to insert into a bucket either causes it to be removed if it was cleared, or update it to the current era. | | `stateManagement.erasWithRemainingBuckets` | The number of eras with tracked buckets. | | `stateManagement.trackedClearOperations` | The number of times the a set of buckets has been cleared, but the removal of those buckets was deferred. - [fact] To check whether a query used block processing, inspect explain output at queryPlanner.winningPlan.slotBasedPlan.stages. A slotBasedPlan field means SBE ran the query. Slow-query logs carry a queryFramework field with value sbe or classic. The docs show no example of what block-processing stages look like. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.2/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying/ · keywords: block processing, index, time series collection, MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing (time series)
- [passage] Due to the unique data structure of time series collections, MongoDB can't efficiently index them for distinct values. Avoid using the [`distinct`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.distinct) command or [`db.collection.distinct()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.distinct.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.distinct) helper method on time series collections. Instead, use a [`$group`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/group.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-group) aggregation to group documents by distinct values, as shown in the following example: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#use-group-instead-of-distinct · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, time series collection, distinct, db.collection.distinct(), $group · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.distinct.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/

- [passage] - **Metadata**: A label or tag that identifies a data series and rarely changes. Metadata is stored in a `metaField`. - [passage] Also, starting in MongoDB 8.0, if you create a time series collection with a shard key containing the `timeField`, a [log message](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-messages-ref) is added to the [log file](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-message-destinations) on the [primary shard](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-shards.md#std-label-primary-shard). In addition, a log message is added every 12 hours on the primary node of the [config server replica set](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-config-servers.md#std-label-csrs). The log messages state that using the `timeField` as a shard key in a time series collection is deprecated and you must reshard your collection using the `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#behavior · keywords: metaField, time series collection, timeField · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/

- [statement] Anti-pattern: using a unique per-device ID (e.g. UUID) as a top-level string metaField makes one bucket per ID per time window (example: 100,000 UUIDs -> 100,000 buckets). - [passage] | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `distanceField` | string | The output field that contains the calculated distance. To specify a field within an embedded document, use [dot notation.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-dot-notation) This field is required for queries on timeseries collections. Starting in MongoDB 8.1, `distanceField` is optional for queries on non-timeseries collections. | | `distanceMultiplier` | number | Optional. The factor to multiply all distances returned by the query. For example, use the `distanceMultiplier` to convert radians, as returned by a spherical query, to kilometers by multiplying by the radius of the Earth. | | `includeLocs` | string | Optional. This specifies the output field that identifies the location used to calculate the distance. This option is useful when a location field contains multiple locations. To specify a field within an embedded document, use [dot notation.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-dot-notation) | | `key` | | Optional. Specify the geospatial indexed field to use when calculating the distance. If your collection has multiple `2d` and/or multiple `2dsphere` indexes, you **must** use the `key` option to specify the indexed field path to use. [Specify Which Geospatial Index to Use](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/geonear.md#std-label-pipeline-geoNear-key-param-example) provides a full example. If there is more than one `2d` index or more than one `2dsphere` index and you do not specify a `key`, MongoDB will return an error. If you do not specify the `key`, and you have at most only one `2d` index and/or only one `2dsphere` index, MongoDB looks first for a `2d` index to use. If a `2d` index does not exists, then MongoDB looks for a `2dsphere` index to use. You must specify the `key` field for `$geoNear` on a time series collection. | | `maxDistance` | number | Optional. The maximum distance from the center point that the documents *can* be. MongoDB limits the results to those documents that fall within the specified distance from the center point. Starting in version 7.2, you can specify a valid constant [expression](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/mql/expressions.md#std-label-aggregation-expressions) that resolves to a number. Specify the distance in meters if the specified point is [GeoJSON](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-GeoJSON) and in radians if the specified point is [legacy coordinate pairs.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-legacy-coordinate-pairs) | | `minDistance` | number | Optional. The minimum distance from the center point that the documents *can* be. MongoDB limits the results to those documents that fall outside the specified distance from the center point. Starting in version 7.2, you can specify a valid constant [expression](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/mql/expressions.md#std-label-aggregation-expressions) that resolves to a number. If using a [2dsphere](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2dsphere.md#std-label-2dsphere-index) index, you can specify the point as either a GeoJSON point or legacy coordinate pair. If using a [2d](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d.md#std-label-2d-index) index, specify the point as a legacy coordinate pair. | | `query` | document | Optional. Limits the results to the documents that match the query. The query syntax is the usual MongoDB [read operation query](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/query-documents.md#std-label-read-operations-query-argument) syntax. You cannot specify a [`$near`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/near.md#mongodb-query-op.-near) predicate in the `query` field of the `$geoNear` stage. You can't use the `query` field for `$geoNear` on a [time series collection.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#std-label-manual-timeseries-landing) | | `spherical` | boolean | Optional. Determines how MongoDB calculates the distance between two points: When `true`, MongoDB uses [`$nearSphere`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/nearsphere.md#mongodb-query-op.-nearSphere) semantics and calculates distances using spherical geometry.; When `false`, MongoDB uses [`$near`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/near.md#mongodb-query-op.-near) semantics: spherical geometry for [2dsphere](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2dsphere.md#std-label-2dsphere-index) indexes and planar geometry for [2d](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d.md#std-label-2d-index) indexes. *Default: false.* | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/geoNear.md#definition · keywords: index, time series collection, distanceField, distanceMultiplier, includeLocs, key
- [passage] For time series collections, TTL indexes also remove a bucket of data when all documents inside it expire. This is equal to the upper timestamp limit of the bucket, plus the `expireAfterSeconds` value. For example, if a bucket covers data up until `2023-03-27T18:29:59Z` and `expireAfterSeconds` is 300, the TTL index expires the bucket after `2023-03-27T18:34:59Z`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl.md#expiration-of-data · keywords: index, time series collection, expireAfterSeconds, 2023-03-27T18:29:59Z, 2023-03-27T18:34:59Z · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/

Larger collections have a greater impact on performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/limits.md#mongodb-atlas-collection-and-index-limits · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] If you cannot stop all writes to the collection during this procedure, do not use the procedure on this page. Instead, build your unique index on the collection by issuing [`db.collection.createIndex()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.createindex.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.createIndex) on the primary for a replica set. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/build-indexes-on-replica-sets.md#unique-indexes · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, db.collection.createIndex()
- [passage] - You cannot create a hashed index on a field that contains an array *or* insert an array into a hashed indexed field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-hashed.md#array-fields · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] - You cannot use hashed indexes in a compound index that becomes a multikey index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-hashed.md#array-fields · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] You cannot specify a [unique constraint](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-unique.md#std-label-index-type-unique) on a hashed index. Instead, you can create an additional non-hashed index with the unique constraint. MongoDB can use that non-hashed index to enforce uniqueness on the chosen field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-hashed.md#unique-constraint · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] If the `$merge` attempts to write a document that violates any unique index on the output collection, the operation generates an error. For example: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#unique-index-constraints · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, $merge
- [passage] - [Fail](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-whenMatched-fail) if there is a matching document in the collection. Specifically, the operation attempts to insert the matching document which violates the unique index on the [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) field(s). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#unique-index-constraints · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] If you specify a modification in the `timeseries` parameter of your `collMod` operation, you cannot use other modification options in the same command. You must perform time series modifications in a dedicated command that is separate from other collection modifications. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collMod.md#modify-time-series-collections · keywords: time series collection, timeseries, collMod
- [passage] | Metrics | Deployment metrics provide insight into hardware performance and database operation efficiency. Atlas collects metrics for your servers, databases, and MongoDB processes and stores metrics data at [various granularity levels](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/monitor-cluster-metrics/#premium-monitoring-granularity). For each granularity level, Atlas computes metrics as averages of the reported metrics at the next finer granularity level. Many metrics have a burst reporting equivalent. You can monitor metrics in the Atlas UI using the Metrics view, Real-Time Performance Panel, Query Profiler, Performance Advisor and Namespace Insights page. You can also use the Atlas CLI or Atlas Administration API to funnel metrics into a tool of your choice. | | --- | --- | | Alerts | Atlas provides alerts for over 200 event types, allowing you to tailor alerts for precise monitoring. Atlas issues alerts for the database and server conditions that you configure in your alert settings. When a condition triggers an alert, Atlas displays a warning symbol on the cluster and sends alert notifications. You can use the Atlas UI, Atlas Administration API, Atlas CLI, and integrated Terraform resource to configure alerts and alert notification. | | Monitoring | Atlas monitoring visualizations provide insights into various key metrics, including hardware performance and database operation efficiency. Tools such as real-time performance panels for network and operation visibility, query profilers for tracking efficiency trends, and automated index suggestions allow you to monitor and troubleshoot issues more effectively, driving greater operational efficiency. For example, these charts can help you understand the impact of server restarts and elections on database performance. | | Logs | Atlas provides logs for each process in the cluster. Each process keeps an account of its activity in its own log file. You can download logs by using the Atlas UI, Atlas CLI, and Atlas Administration API. To learn more, see [Guidance for Atlas Auditing and Logging.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/auditing-logging.md#std-label-arch-center-auditing-logging) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/monitoring-alerts.md#features-for-atlas-monitoring-and-alerts · keywords: index, metaField
- [passage] You cannot create [partial indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#std-label-index-type-partial) on the metaField and timeField. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md#partial-indexes · keywords: index, metaField
- [passage] You cannot create sparse indexes on the metaField. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md#prohibited-indexes · keywords: index, metaField
- [passage] | **MongoDB Version** | **Changes** | | --- | --- | | 6.1 | Slow operation log messages include [cache refresh time fields.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-messages-cache-refresh-times) | | 6.2 | Slow operation log messages include a `queryFramework` field that indicates which query engine executed the query: `queryFramework: "classic"` indicates that the classic engine executed the query.; `queryFramework: "sbe"` indicates that the slot-based query execution engine executed the query. | | 6.3 | Slow operation log messages and [database profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#std-label-profiler) entries include a `cpuNanos` field that specifies the total CPU time spent by a query operation in nanoseconds. The `cpuNanos` field is only available on Linux systems. | | 7.0 (and 6.0.13, 5.0.24) | The `totalOplogSlotDurationMicros` in the slow query log message shows the time between a write operation getting a commit timestamp to commit the storage engine writes and actually committing. `mongod` supports parallel writes. However, it commits write operations with commit timestamps in any order. For example, consider the following writes with commit timestamps: writeA with Timestamp1; writeB with Timestamp2; writeC with Timestamp3 Suppose writeB commits first at Timestamp2. Replication is paused until writeA commits because writeA's oplog entry with Timestamp1 is required for replication to copy the oplog to secondary replica set members. | | 8.0 | The slow query output includes a `queues` document that contains information about the operation's [queues](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/serverstatus.md#std-label-server-status-queues). Each queue in the `queues` field contains a `totalTimeQueuedMicros` field that contains the total cumulative time in microseconds that the operation spent in the corresponding queue. The `queryShapeHash` field for a [query shape](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-shapes.md#std-label-query-shapes) is also included in the slow query log when available. If a command with a specific query shape is [rejected](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/operation-rejection-filters.md#std-label-operation-rejection-filters), MongoDB logs a message that states the query command was rejected. The message contains the query namespace, `queryShapeHash`, and the command with the rejected query. MongoDB only logs the message if the log verbosity level is set to at least `2`. | | 8.1 | Slow query log messages contain new metrics if the query execution writes temporary files to disk. These metrics are prefixed by the query execution stage that caused the query to exceed the memory limit. For example, `sortSpills` indicates the number of times that the sort stage of query execution wrote temporary files to disk. `<executionPart>Spills` indicates the number of times the corresponding query execution stage wrote temporary files to disk.; `<executionPart>SpilledBytes` indicates the size, in bytes, of the memory released by writing temporary files to disk.; `<executionPart>SpilledDataStorageSize` indicates the size, in bytes, of disk space used for temporary files.; `<executionPart>SpilledRecords` indicates the number of records written to temporary files on disk. For more information on writing temporary files to disk, see [`allowDiskUse()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) | | 8.3 | Slow query log entries have an optional `originalQueryShapeHash` field that contains that query shape of the following operations that originate on the [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#std-program-mongos) : [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find); [`aggregate`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/aggregate.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.aggregate); [`count`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/count.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.count); [`distinct`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.distinct) The original query shape of the `mongos` operation may differ after the `mongos` sends the operation to the [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#std-program-mongod) . MongoDB 8.3 also introduces slow in-progress query log entries. Queries trigger a slow-in progress log during execution. These logs contain less information than standard slow query logs. MongoDB logs queries at most once if the query's duration surpasses the [`operationProfiling.slowOpInProgressThresholdMs`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-operationProfiling.slowOpInProgressThresholdMs) When an operation specifies a [time limit for a query](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/query-documents/specify-query-timeout.md#std-label-manual-query-timeout), slow query logs contain a `deadline` field. `deadline` indicates the time the operation must complete by, which is equal to the time at the start of the operation plus the value of the query timeout. | | 9.0 | When a query shape has query knobs set through [`setQuerySettings`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setQuerySettings) or [`setParameter`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setparameter.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setParameter), slow query log entries include a `queryKnobs` document. The document shows the effective value of each knob and where the value comes from, with the same shape as the [explain output](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-output-query-knobs). For details, see [Query Knobs.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#std-label-setQuerySettings-query-knobs) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#version-specific-changes · keywords: index, metaField, queryFramework, queryFramework: "classic", queryFramework: "sbe", cpuNanos
- [passage] If MongoDB cannot obtain the sort order with an index scan, then MongoDB uses a top-k sort algorithm. This algorithm buffers the first `k` results (or last, depending on the sort order) seen so far by the underlying index or collection access. If the memory footprint of these `k` results exceeds 100 megabytes, MongoDB automatically writes temporary files to disk unless the query specifies [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) with a value of `false` (in which case, the query fails). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.sort.md#limit-results · keywords: index, working set for time series, cursor.allowDiskUse(), false
- [passage] Limits the amount of memory that simultaneous [index builds](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-creation.md#std-label-index-build-process) on one collection may consume for their duration. The specified amount of memory is shared between all indexes built using a single [`createIndexes`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/createindexes.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.createIndexes) command or its shell helper [`db.collection.createIndexes()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.createindexes.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.createIndexes). Increasing the limit may avoid negative performance impacts in some cases, such as when building numerous indexes simultaneously with a single [`createIndexes`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/createindexes.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.createIndexes) command and/or when working with index key data set sizes that exceed 500GB. The memory consumed by an index build is separate from the WiredTiger cache memory (see [`cacheSizeGB`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/configuration-options.md#mongodb-setting-storage.wiredTiger.engineConfig.cacheSizeGB)). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#general-parameters · keywords: index, working set for time series, createIndexes, db.collection.createIndexes(), cacheSizeGB
- [passage] Rolling indexes build indexes on the applicable nodes sequentially and may reduce the performance impact of an index build if your deployment's average CPU utilization exceeds (N-1)/N-10% where N is the number of CPU threads available to mongod of if the WiredTiger cache fill ratio regularly exceeds 90%. If your deployment does not meet this criteria, use the default index build. You can't create a rolling index on an M0 free cluster or M2/M5 shared cluster. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cli/current/command/atlas-api-rollingIndex.md · keywords: index, working set for time series

- [passage] Some high-latency [`$lookup`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/lookup.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-lookup) operations don't generate a slow query log for the foreign collection. This can occur because slow query logs correspond with operations that are reported in the [Query Profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/query-profiler.md#std-label-query-profiler), whereas latency metrics increment only when a [collection lock](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/faq/concurrency.md#std-label-faq-concurrency-locking) is acquired. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/namespace-insights.md#high-latency-lookup-operations · keywords: metaField cardinality, $lookup · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/query-profiler.md
- [passage] If the `$lookup` query on a shard can perform a local read, the `$lookup` doesn't record a separate operation for querying the foreign collection. A local read refers to when the query on the foreign collection targets only the same shard where the current operation is being executed. As a result, the `$lookup` operation increases the Namespace Insights latency metrics and operation counts, but does not generate a slow query log for the foreign collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/namespace-insights.md#high-latency-lookup-operations · keywords: metaField cardinality, $lookup · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/query-profiler.md
- [passage] Avoid increasing the WiredTiger internal cache size above its default value. If your case requires to do so, you can use `--wiredTigerCacheSizePct` to account for changes in memory due to vertical. You must specify a percentage of up to 80% of available memory. Calculated values can range from 0.256GB to 10000GB. For example, on a system with 2GB of RAM the `--wiredTigerCacheSizePct` cannot be set to 10 because 10% of 2GB is 0.2 GB, which is less than 0.256GB. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#cache-configuration-settings · keywords: metaField cardinality, --wiredTigerCacheSizePct
- [passage] When running MongoDB servers and clients on NUMA hardware, you should configure a memory interleave policy so that the host behaves in a non-NUMA fashion. If the NUMA configuration may degrade performance, MongoDB prints a warning. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/production-notes.md#mongodb-and-numa-hardware · keywords: metaField cardinality

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [fact] Because data is indexed per bucket by metaField rather than one index entry per data point, MongoDB docs say time series indexes are much smaller than on regular collections, which improves WiredTiger in-memory cache use. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/ · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series
- [passage] Starting in version 6.0, you can add a secondary index to any field in a time series collection. MongoDB indexes time series collections by [buckets](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#std-label-timeseries-bucketing) of documents as opposed to individual documents. Time series buckets contain documents with shared metaField values, ordered by timeField values that are close together. MongoDB indexes the minimum and maximum values of all fields, except the metaField. Indexing buckets instead of individual documents reduces index size and improves query efficiency. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [passage] Compared to normal collections, storing time series data in time series collections improves query efficiency and reduces the disk usage for time series data and [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index). MongoDB 6.3 and later automatically creates a [compound index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#std-label-index-type-compound) on the time and metadata fields for new time series collections. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#benefits · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/
- [fact] Since MongoDB 6.0 a secondary index can be added to any field of a time series collection. The server indexes buckets rather than individual documents, and stores the min and max of every field except the metaField, which reduces index size. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [statement] MongoDB's blog (published 2024-12-09, updated 2025-07-21) claims 10-40x improvements across workloads, up to 100x for some large aggregations, and 20x ops/sec versus 7.0 in a worked example. The example ran on an Atlas M50 using MongoDB's TSBS fork: about 6 million events, a 24-hour $match, $sort, $group with $dateTrunc, $setWindowFields and $expMovingAvg. — https://mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/key-enhancements-mongodb-8-0-block-processing · keywords: block processing, time series collection, time series query, MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing (time series)
- [fact] SERVER-79136: a $match followed by $group on the metaField with $min/$max was rewritten to use bucket-level control.min/control.max, ignoring the filter, so results were wrong (5 instead of 21 in the report). Affected 6.0.8 and 7.0.0-rc8; fixed in 5.0.20, 6.0.9, 7.0.0-rc9 and 7.1.0-rc0. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-79136 · keywords: metaField, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [passage] MongoDB reorders the `metaField` of time-series collections, which may cause servers to store data in a different field order than applications. If a `metaField` is an object, queries on the `metaField` may produce inconsistent results because `metaField` order may vary between servers and applications. To optimize queries on a time-series `metaField`, query the `metaField` on scalar sub-fields rather than the entire `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#query-the-metafield-on-sub-fields · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/

- [passage] To update the custom bucketing fields `bucketRoundingSeconds` and `bucketMaxSpanSeconds` instead of `granularity`, include both custom fields in the `collMod` command and set them to the same value: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collMod.md#modify-time-series-collections · keywords: metaField, time series collection, bucketRoundingSeconds, bucketMaxSpanSeconds, granularity, collMod · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md
- [passage] Delta Encoding takes advantage of the data in your time series collection having time-series characteristics. Instead of storing absolute values, Delta Encoding assumes that the measurements will not change rapidly between each other. This approach reduces the amount of information required by only storing the difference between measurements. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-compression.md#delta-encoding-delta-compression · keywords: time series collection, working set for time series
- [passage] MongoDB groups documents with matching `ticker` values. Instead of having to check for matches across all fields in all documents, the server only has to check against the `metaField`, in this case `ticker`, to narrow down the search range to a unique time series. This fits the expected use case, which is searching for activity on a single stock. A user searching for information on MongoDB stock (MDB) doesn't need to consider results for Amazon (AMZN). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying.md#querying-the-metafield · keywords: metaField, time series collection, ticker
- [passage] Starting in version 8.0, MongoDB may execute certain time series queries using block processing. This performance improvement processes queries in "blocks" of data, rather than individual values. Block processing improves query execution speed and throughput when working with time series collections. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying.md#block-processing · keywords: block processing, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/sbe.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.2/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying/
- [passage] For example, if you have two sensors that correspond to two `metaField` values, `sensor A` and `sensor B`, a batch that contains multiple measurements from a single sensor incurs the cost of one insert, rather than one insert per measurement. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#batch-document-writes · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, sensor A, sensor B · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [fact] Insert tip for many metaField values: batch documents with identical metaField together in insertMany with ordered:false, so one insert cost is paid per metaField value rather than per document. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [fact] Query tip: MongoDB reorders object metaField contents, so query scalar sub-fields (e.g. metaField.sensorId) rather than equality on the whole metaField object. Arrays as metaField may behave unexpectedly because array equality is order-dependent. The metaField field itself cannot be redefined after creation. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [passage] Time series collections use [zstd](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-zstd) compression, which differs from the global default compression algorithm, [snappy.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-snappy) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-compression.md#default-compression-algorithm · keywords: time series collection, working set for time series
- [passage] MongoDB does not create an index on the `_id` field when you create a time series collection. This differs from regular collections which have an index on the `_id` field by default. Commands that specify a hint on the `_id` field on time series collections return an error unless you manually create an index on the `_id` field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#default-index · keywords: index, time series collection, _id
- [passage] Indexes improve read performance, but a large number of indexes can negatively impact write performance since indexes must be updated during writes. If your collection already has several indexes, consider this tradeoff of read and write performance when deciding whether to create new indexes. Examine whether a query for such a collection can be modified to take advantage of existing indexes, as well as whether a query occurs often enough to justify the cost of a new index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/performance-advisor.md#index-considerations · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] You can have a clustered index and add [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index) to a clustered collection. Clustered indexes differ from secondary indexes: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#behavior · keywords: index, secondary index on time series
- [passage] Prior to MongoDB 6.0.7, if a [secondary index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index) existed on a clustered collection and the secondary index was usable by your query, the query planner selected the secondary index instead of the clustered index by default. In MongoDB 6.1 and prior, to use the clustered index, you must provide a hint because the [query optimizer](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-plans.md#std-label-query-plans-query-optimization) does not automatically select the clustered index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#behavior · keywords: index, secondary index on time series
- [fact] Allegro's 5.0.3 benchmark found aggregation over a random six-hour window 23-48% faster on a time series collection than a regular one (10K to 100K queries), but single-timestamp lookups were nearly equal (16.854s vs 16.038s for 1M queries). — https://blog.allegro.tech/2021/12/performance-evaluation-of-timeseries.html · keywords: time series collection, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns
- [passage] - To avoid network roundtrips, use a single [`insertMany()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.insertmany.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.insertMany) statement as opposed to multiple [`insertOne()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.insertone.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.insertOne) statements. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#batch-document-writes · keywords: metaField cardinality, insertMany(), insertOne()
- [passage] Applications may target different members of a replica set. As such, each replica set member might receive different read commands and have plan cache information that differs from other members. Nevertheless, running `$planCacheStats` on a replica set or a sharded cluster obeys the normal read preference rules. That is, on a replica set, the operation gathers plan cache information from just one member of replica set, and on a sharded cluster, the operation gathers plan cache information from just one member of each shard replica set. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/planCacheStats.md#read-preference · keywords: metaField cardinality, $planCacheStats

- [passage] In MongoDB 6.3 and later, instead of `granularity`, you can set bucket boundaries manually using the two custom bucketing parameters. Consider this approach if you expect to query data for fixed time intervals, such as every 4 hours starting at midnight. Ensuring buckets don't overlap between those periods optimizes for high query volume and [`insert`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/insert.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.insert) operations. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#using-custom-bucketing-parameters · keywords: metaField, granularity, insert
- [passage] For the weather station example, if you generate summary reports every 4 hours, you could adjust bucketing by setting the custom bucketing parameters to 14400 seconds instead of using a `granularity` of `"minutes"`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#using-custom-bucketing-parameters · keywords: metaField, granularity, "minutes"
- [passage] Horizontal Scaling involves dividing the system dataset and load over multiple servers, adding more servers to increase capacity as required. Each machine handles a subset of the overall workload, which can cost less than high-end hardware for a single machine. The trade-off is increased complexity in infrastructure and maintenance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sharding/ · keywords: working set for time series

## Facts and statements

- [passage] The following command creates a compound secondary index on `metaField` (ascending) and `timeField` (descending): — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, timeField
- [passage] The following last point query example uses the descending `timeField` compound secondary index created above: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, timeField
- [fact] Last-point queries (latest reading per metaField value) are served by compound indexes on the metaField and timeField in any direction. They are fastest with the DISTINCT_SCAN optimization, which needs a descending timeField index, for example {metadata.sensorId: 1, timestamp: -1}. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] SERVER-63279: pushing a metaField predicate past a stage that changes document contents (for example $project) returned wrong results. Affected 5.0.5 and 5.2.0; fixed in 5.0.7, 5.2.2 and 5.3.0. After the fix, a $match placed after a document-reshaping stage may stay after the unpack and cost more. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-63279 · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [statement] SERVER-96923, a bounded sort optimization for time series queries that do not sort on timeField, is an unresolved backlog feature request (last updated 2026-09-25), so such sorts are not guaranteed to be bounded. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-96923 · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns
- [passage] In time series data, a last point query returns the data point with the latest timestamp for a given field. For time series collections, a last point query fetches the latest measurement for each unique metadata value. For example, you may want to get the latest temperature reading from all sensors. Improve performance on last point queries by creating any of the following indexes: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query
- [passage] If the `queryPlanner.winningPlan.inputStage.stage` is either `CLUSTERED_IXSCAN` or `IXSCAN`, the index was used. For more information on the explain plan output, see [Explain Results.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-results) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, queryPlanner.winningPlan.inputStage.stage, CLUSTERED_IXSCAN
- [passage] The `winningPlan.queryPlan.inputStage.stage` is `DISTINCT_SCAN`, which indicates that the index was used. For more information on the explain plan output, see [Explain Results.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-results) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#last-point-queries-on-time-series-collections · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, winningPlan.queryPlan.inputStage.stage, DISTINCT_SCAN
- [passage] - You can only create [multikey indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey.md#std-label-index-type-multikey) on the `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#time-series-secondary-indexes · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [passage] - You can only create [2d indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d.md#std-label-2d-index) on the `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#time-series-secondary-indexes · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [passage] - You can only create [sparse indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) on the `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#time-series-secondary-indexes · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [fact] The default compound index covers the whole metaField subdocument, so it is only used for $eq on the metaField. To serve other predicates such as $in, create a secondary index on specific metaField subfields, for example metadata.type. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] Guidance on field roles: use the metaField index for filtering and equality, and use the timeField and other indexed fields for range queries. If timeField values fall before 1970-01-01 or after 2038-01-19, create an index on the timeField to keep queries fast. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [statement] A forum workaround sorts system.buckets.<name> on control.max.timestamp and then looks up the document in the view. One reader reported that control.max.timestamp did not return the true latest record in their data, so the workaround can be wrong with out-of-order ingest. — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/time-series-how-to-get-the-most-recent-document/149455 · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] The optimizer pushes $match predicates past $_internalUnpackBucket: predicates on the metaField push down exactly, $lt on a measurement becomes $lt on control.min in the bucket predicate, and $geoWithin becomes $_internalBucketGeoWithin. The same logic is reused to translate partial index filters into bucket-level filters. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-59163 · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [fact] Put metaField and time-range $match stages first in the pipeline, and index the metaField (and time) fields. A leading $match on indexed meta fields restricts the buckets that get unpacked; a compound index on meta subfields supports a $match then $group pattern in place of distinct(). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [passage] For more information and examples, see [Add Secondary Indexes to Time Series Collections.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md#indexing-best-practices · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, secondary index on time series, time series collection
- [passage] Sort operations on time series collections can use secondary indexes on the `timeField` field. Under certain conditions, sort operations can also use compound secondary indexes on the `metaField` and `timeField` fields. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#use-secondary-indexes-to-improve-sort-performance · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, timeField
- [passage] Time series collections support [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md#std-label-timeseries-add-secondary-index) on the field specified as the `metaField`. If the data model of your time series data does not have a designated field for your metadata, you can transform your data to create one. To transform the data in your existing collection, use [`$out`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-out) to create a temporary collection with your time series data. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-migrate-with-tools.md#steps · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, $out
- [passage] Using the `metaField` to shard your collection provides sufficienct cardinality as a shard key for time series collections. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#use-the-metafield-as-your-shard-key · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection, time series sharding · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] Starting in MongoDB 6.3: if you create a new time series collection, MongoDB also generates a compound index on the metaField and timeField fields. To improve query performance, queries on time series collections use the new compound index. The compound index also uses the optimized storage format. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/ · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md
- [statement] 2dsphere indexes can be created on the timeField, metaField or measurement fields since 6.0, per the secondary index page. The OneUptime blog says they are supported only on metaField subfields. Time series collections support only $geoNear for sorting by distance; $near and $nearSphere do not work. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-secondary-index.md · keywords: index, metaField, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series
- [fact] SERVER-100910: for compound time series indexes the planner's sortMatchesTraversalPreference always returned false, so reversed-direction (backward scan) plans were not generated and sorts could miss the bounded sort optimization. Closed Fixed in 9.0.0-rc0 on 2026-05-14; earlier versions are affected. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-100910 · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Sort and Range Query Patterns

- [fact] Block processing applies to aggregation pipelines that begin with $match, with $sort on the timeField only, or with $group. A MongoDB blog also names $setWindowFields as an analytical stage that benefits, but gives no complete list of supported operators. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.2/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying/ · keywords: block processing, metaField, time series collection, MongoDB 8.0 Block Processing (time series)
- [fact] Each bucket stores control.min and control.max for the time field and measurements, which lets range queries skip buckets that fall entirely outside the query range before unpacking. — https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-time-series-buckets/view · keywords: metaField, time series collection, time series query, Time-Series Bucket Unpacking and $match Pushdown
- [passage] The number of buckets in a time series collection depends on the number of unique `metaField` values. Collections with fine-grained or dynamic `metaField` values may generate more, sparsely packed, short-lived buckets than collections with simple `metaField` values that rarely or never change. Fine-grained and dynamic `metaField` values typically decrease storage and query effiency. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#metafield-considerations · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/

- [fact] Granularity mismatch inflates bucket count or traversal cost: granularity 'hours' for 5-minute data puts up to a month of events in one bucket (slower queries); 'seconds' creates many single-document buckets. Granularity or bucketing span can later be increased but not decreased. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/ · keywords: metaField, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series
- [passage] If an [embedded data model](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/embedding.md#std-label-data-modeling-embedding) supports your application's needs, use nested fields. - [statement] Compression best practices (omit empty fields, round numerics, keep consistent field order) reduce on-disk bucket size; schema changes between documents leave following documents uncompressed. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/ · keywords: metaField cardinality, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series

- [fact] Collection data in the WiredTiger cache is uncompressed, so block compression saves disk but not cache space; the OS filesystem cache holds the compressed on-disk form. Compressed time series storage size therefore understates the cache footprint of hot buckets. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/faq/storage/ · keywords: index, time series collection, working set for time series, Working Set Sizing for Time Series

- [passage] Starting in MongoDB 7.0, you can create partial TTL indexes on [time series collections](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#std-label-manual-timeseries-landing). These indexes use the collection `timeField` as the key field, and require a [partial filter expression](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#std-label-index-type-partial) on the `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl.md#create-a-ttl-index · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, timeField · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/
- [passage] Time series collections include an optional `expireAfterSeconds` field. If you don't set `expireAfterSeconds`, a TTL index with a `partialFilterExpression` lets you set an expiration period for documents that match the filter. If you do set `expireAfterSeconds`, a partial TTL index lets you set a different, shorter expiration period for matching documents. You can only create a `partialFilterExpression` on the `metaField`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl.md#create-a-ttl-index · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection, expireAfterSeconds, partialFilterExpression · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md

- [passage] If there are [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index) on [time series collections](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#std-label-manual-timeseries-collection) and you need to downgrade the feature compatibility version (FCV), you must first drop any secondary indexes that are incompatible with the downgraded FCV. - [passage] Compare this to a time series collection. Time series collections write data in order, meaning recent transactions can be kept in memory for much faster retrieval. Since they are written in sequence, documents are stored together, so there's no need to read every disk block after a document is no longer in memory. Data is indexed by the `metaField`, leading to much smaller indexes. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#comparing-time-series-collections-to-regular-collections · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] MongoDB automatically creates a [compound index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#std-label-index-type-compound) on both the metaField and timeField of a time series collection. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#indexes · keywords: index, metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/
- [fact] Before downgrading the feature compatibility version, drop every time series secondary index that the lower FCV does not support. Otherwise the downgrade is blocked. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-index.md · keywords: index, secondary index on time series, time series collection, Secondary Indexes on Time Series

- [passage] Internally, MongoDB optimizes time series data by grouping documents in a time series collection based on common `metaField` values. Selecting a useful one provides significant optimizations to storage density and query performance. For more information, see [metaFields.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#std-label-timeseries-collections-metafield) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md · keywords: metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] - An identical `metaField` value, which should uniquely identify a time series. If a `metaField` is an object or array, MongoDB groups only if all object fields or array elements match. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#how-bucketing-works · keywords: metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] - `timeField` values that are close together. The time series collection's `granularity`, `bucketMaxSpanSeconds`, and `bucketRoundingSeconds` parameters control the time span covered by each bucket. For more information, see [Set Granularity for Time Series Data.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#std-label-timeseries-granularity) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#how-bucketing-works · keywords: metaField, time series collection, timeField, granularity, bucketMaxSpanSeconds, bucketRoundingSeconds · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] You can modify a time series collection's granularity, but only to change from finer to coarser measurements, such as extending bucket coverage from minutes to hours. This doesn't change how data is stored across existing buckets. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#how-bucketing-works · keywords: metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] The starting timestamp of a new bucket is rounded down based on the collection's [granularity](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#std-label-timeseries-granularity). This handles cases where documents with out-of-order timestamps arrive in close succession. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#creation · keywords: metaField, time series collection · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing/
- [passage] - Time has moved forward or backward past the covered time span, as indicated by an incoming document timestamp that falls outside of the bucket's bounds. These bounds are determined by the collection's [granularity](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#std-label-timeseries-granularity) setting. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-bucketing.md#closure · keywords: metaField, time series collection

- [passage] MongoDB doesn't guarantee that expired data will be deleted immediately upon expiration. Once all documents in a bucket are expired, the background task that removes expired buckets removes the bucket during the next run. The maximum span of time that a single bucket is allowed to cover is controlled by the `granularity` of the time series collection: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-automatic-removal.md#timing-of-delete-operations · keywords: metaField, time series collection, granularity

- [passage] You can increase `timeseries.granularity` from a shorter unit of time to a longer one using a [`collMod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collmod.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.collMod) command. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-granularity.md#change-time-series-granularity · keywords: metaField, time series collection, timeseries.granularity, collMod
- [passage] The second major dimension for querying time series data is time. Since MongoDB groups documents that have both an identical `metaField` value and close `timeField` values, this further narrows the scope of a query to a range of buckets. Recent transactions are kept in memory, so it's easy to stream data in real time. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-querying.md#querying-the-timefield · keywords: metaField, time series collection, timeField
- [passage] Read operations on time series collections with read concern `"snapshot"` guarantee snapshot isolation only in the absence of concurrent drop or rename operations on collections in the read operation. Re-creating a time series collection on the same namespace with different granularity setting does not yield full snapshot isolation. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#snapshot-isolation · keywords: metaField, time series collection, "snapshot"
- [passage] Your choice of `metaField` has the biggest impact on optimizing queries in your application. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#set-a-strategic-metafield-when-creating-the-collection · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] You can improve performance by setting the `granularity` or custom bucketing parameters to the best match for the time span between incoming measurements from the same data source. For example, if you are recording weather data from thousands of sensors but only record data from each sensor once per 5 minutes, you can either set `granularity` to `"minutes"` or set the custom bucketing parameters to `300` (seconds). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md#set-appropriate-bucket-granularity · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, granularity, "minutes", 300 · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices/
- [passage] Once you set a collection's `granularity` or the custom bucketing parameters `bucketMaxSpanSeconds` and `bucketRoundingSeconds`, you can increase the time span covered by a bucket, but not decrease it. Use the [`collMod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collmod.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.collMod) command to modify the parameters. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-limitations.md#modifying-bucket-parameters · keywords: metaField, working set for time series, granularity, bucketMaxSpanSeconds, bucketRoundingSeconds, collMod

- [fact] Fine-grained or changing metaField values generate many sparsely packed, short-lived buckets, increasing collection cardinality and decreasing storage and query efficiency (official docs; no numeric threshold given). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [fact] Docs' metaField rules: choose fields that rarely or never change; prefer stable identifiers common in filters; do not put fields not used for filtering in the metaField, store them as measurements. The docs say the metaField choice has the biggest impact on query optimization. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-best-practices.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns
- [fact] Scoping: docs state the compressed bucket format in cache 'supports high cardinality workloads while preserving efficient query performance', so high cardinality is not prohibited; the penalty applies mainly to sparse/short-lived buckets from fine-grained or changing values. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md · keywords: metaField, metaField cardinality, metaField Cardinality Anti-Patterns

- [passage] MongoDB uses column compression on each nested field individually, which provides the same compression quality as flattening the fields to the top level. - [passage] Each [`mongod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongod.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongod) in the replica set or sharded cluster *must* have [featureCompatibilityVersion](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setfeaturecompatibilityversion.md#std-label-set-fcv) set to at least `4.4` to start index builds simultaneously across replica set members. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/createIndexes.md#replica-sets-and-sharded-clusters · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, mongod, 4.4
- [passage] Index builds on a replica set or sharded cluster build simultaneously across all data-bearing replica set members. For sharded clusters, the index build occurs only on shards containing data for the collection being indexed. - [passage] If the output collection does not exist, `$merge` requires the [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) identifier to be the `_id` field. For example, if the output collection `newDailyCommentCount` does not exist and you want to specify the `commentDate` field as the [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) identifier: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#create-a-new-collection-if-output-collection-is-non-existent · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, $merge, _id, on, newDailyCommentCount

- [passage] If the unique index used by `$merge` for [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) field(s) is dropped mid-aggregation, there is no guarantee that the aggregation will be killed. - [passage] - [Insert a non-matching document](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-whenNotMatched-insert) that violates a unique index other than the index on the [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) field(s). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#unique-index-constraints · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] - [Replace an existing document](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-whenMatched-replace) with a new document that violates a unique index other than the index on the [on](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#std-label-merge-on) field(s). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge.md#unique-index-constraints · keywords: index, metaField cardinality
- [passage] - If `$in` has fewer than 201 array elements, the elements are expanded and then merged in the sort order specified for the index using a `SORT_MERGE` stage. This improves performance for small arrays. In this case, `$in` is similar to an equality predicate with ESR. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md#additional-considerations · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, $in, SORT_MERGE
- [passage] - If `$in` has 201 elements or more, the elements are ordered like a range operator. In this case, the performance improvement for small arrays isn't realized. It isn't possible for the subsequent fields in the index to be used for sorting, and `$in` is similar to a range predicate with ESR. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md#additional-considerations · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, $in
- [passage] - If you typically use `$in` operators with small arrays, include them earlier in the index specification. If you typically use large arrays, include `$in` operators where you would include a range predicate. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md#additional-considerations · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, $in
- [passage] - `metadata`: The estimate comes from database metadata like collection cardinality. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#unsharded-collections · keywords: index, metaField cardinality, metadata · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results/

- [passage] For physical servers using spinning disks, the operating system should use the *mq-deadline* scheduler. - [passage] - Uses [`$dateTrunc`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#mongodb-expression-exp.-dateTrunc) to truncate each document's `date` to the appropriate month. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-aggregations-operators.md#calculate-average-price-per-month · keywords: time series query, $dateTrunc, date
- [passage] By default, `granularity` is set to `seconds`. You can improve performance by setting the `granularity` value to the closest match to the time span between incoming measurements from the same data source. For example, if you are recording weather data from thousands of sensors but only record data from each sensor once per 5 minutes, set `granularity` to `"minutes"`. The less frequently you append new documents, the greater the storage and performance benefits of coarser granularity. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries/timeseries-considerations.md#granularity · keywords: metaField, granularity, seconds, "minutes"
- [passage] Together, [binSize](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#std-label-dateTrunc-binSize) and [unit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#std-label-dateTrunc-unit) specify the time period used in the [`$dateTrunc`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#mongodb-expression-exp.-dateTrunc) calculation. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/dateTrunc.md#binsize-and-unit-fields · keywords: time series query, $dateTrunc

For example, if [binSize](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#std-label-dateTrunc-binSize) is `10` and [unit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#std-label-dateTrunc-unit) is `year`, example time periods are: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/dateTrunc.md#binsize-and-unit-fields · keywords: time series query, week, $dateTrunc, 2000-01-01T00:00:00.00Z, 10, year
- [passage] - Equal to `week`, [`$dateTrunc`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#mongodb-expression-exp.-dateTrunc) uses a reference date that is set to the earliest first day of the week that is greater than or equal to `2000-01-01`. The first day is set using [startOfWeek](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/datetrunc.md#std-label-dateTrunc-startOfWeek) (the default is Sunday). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/dateTrunc.md#binsize-and-unit-fields · keywords: time series query, week, $dateTrunc, 2000-01-01

- [passage] In the worst case, running metadata compaction reveals the number of unique field/value pairs inserted across all documents since the previous compaction. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#scheduling-metadata-compaction · keywords: working set for time series
- [passage] For details on the exact information revealed by metadata compaction, see "Section 6: Theoretical Analysis" and "Section 9: Guidelines" in MongoDB's [Queryable Encryption Technical Paper](https://www.mongodb.com/collateral/queryable-encryption-technical-paper). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#scheduling-metadata-compaction · keywords: working set for time series
- [passage] - `docinserts`: the number of documents inserted since the last compaction. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#scheduling-metadata-compaction · keywords: working set for time series, docinserts
- [passage] - `valinserts`: the number of unique field/value pairs inserted since the last compaction. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#scheduling-metadata-compaction · keywords: working set for time series, valinserts
- [passage] The number of encrypted fields per document multiplied by the number of insertions since last compaction, minus the number of unique field/value pairs inserted across all documents since the last compaction, should be greater than or equal to the number of documents to remove from the `ESC`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#scheduling-metadata-compaction · keywords: working set for time series, ESC
- [passage] The formula would be satisfied, for example, if 200 documents were inserted since the last compaction with a total of 200 unique field/value pairs across all documents, or if 400 documents were inserted since the last compaction with 700 unique field/value pairs. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/queryable-encryption/fundamentals/manage-collections.md#example · keywords: working set for time series
- [passage] You must run metadata compaction manually.
